---
title: Results
---

Mosaic is a benchmark for differentiable solvers. It measures whether they are
fit for purpose and at what cost, in compute and in development effort. Because
every solver runs the same setups under the same protocol, Mosaic also allows
researchers to investigate patterns across solvers, for example between solvers
that share numerical characteristics, or between gradient quality and
optimization performance. [Our paper](paper.qmd) is one such investigation.

This page shows, for each setup, whether each solver's forward solution,
gradient and optimization results meet the setup's criteria, what the solver
costs relative to its peers, and what it took to make it run. The
[Overview](index.qmd#evaluation-protocol) describes how the experiments work.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
These are **example results**, produced automatically on GitHub-hosted runners
and refreshed on every release. Wall-clock times vary between runs, so read
them for relative scaling between solvers. Accuracy and gradient metrics change
little across hardware. For numbers that reflect *your* setup, [run the
benchmark yourself](getting-started.qmd) on your target hardware.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Results describe the wrappers"}
Each solver runs in a wrapper written by the Mosaic team or its contributors,
so a flag or a slow time describes how *this wrapper* behaves on *this setup*.
What it took to make a solver run a setup is part of the result. Each solver's
interventions and deviations are recorded with their reasons and evidence in
the [solver reference](solvers.qmd), and summarized in the **Effort** and
**Deviations** columns below. If you maintain or use one of these solvers and
can improve its configuration, [contributions are welcome](contributing.qmd).
:::

## Setups {#setups}

A setup is one problem statement, such as periodic Taylor–Green flow or channel
flow past a cylinder. Setups of the same physics are reported separately,
because a solver that handles one need not handle the other. Each setup has its
own results page with every experiment and plot.

## How to read the results {#how-to-read-the-results}

For each setup, each solver gets the following.

- **Forward, gradient and optimization checks.** Every experiment carries pass
  criteria set in its problem configuration (`status_check`), for example an
  error bound against the reference, a finite-difference agreement bound for
  the gradient, or the fraction of the objective an optimizer must remove. A
  check combines the setup's *gate* experiments for that suite. It is shown as
  *Partial* with a count when the solver passed the gates it ran but did not
  run all of them. An optimization check also shows after how many
  iterations the loss levelled off, that is, made 95% of its total
  improvement on a log scale. Hover over a check for each gate's headline
  numbers.
- **Cost**, forward and VJP: wall-clock time as a multiple of the fastest
  solver *on the same kind of device*, at the largest problem size every solver
  in that group completed. GPU and CPU solvers ran on different machines, so
  they are compared within their group only. A **≈** marks a gap to the fastest
  solver that is no larger than twice the spread of the two solvers' timed
  trials, so the two cannot be told apart on this run. The results page of each
  setup gives the absolute times.
- **Peak memory** of the VJP pass at the same problem size (of the forward pass
  for forward-only solvers): device memory for GPU solvers, including the CUDA
  context and allocator pools, and the container's memory for CPU solvers.
- **Reliability**: how many of the setup's experiments ran cleanly, out of
  those the solver supports. It also counts diagnostic experiments that are not
  gates, such as Jacobian spectra, horizon sweeps and cost sweeps. The notes
  below each table name every flag, exclusion and resource limit behind it.
- **Effort**: the highest level among the interventions a solver *needs* on
  that setup. L0 means nothing beyond expected tweaks, that is, the public API
  with its defaults or documented options such as a tolerance. L1 is
  undocumented configuration, L2 user code on the library's public primitives,
  and L3 changes to the solver itself.
- **Deviations**: the places where a solver runs a substitute for the
  prescribed setup, such as a different outflow condition. Reliability says how
  cleanly the solver ran the setup as wrapped, and deviations say where the
  wrapped setup differs from the prescribed one, so read the two together.

Effort and deviation cells link to the solver's record, which lists every
intervention with its reason, evidence and upstream issue, including
interventions whose reason is not yet known.

::: {.ck-legend}
| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [✓ Pass]{.ck .ck-pass} | Every gate experiment met its criteria. |
| [✓ Partial]{.ck .ck-pass} | The gates that ran met their criteria, but not all of them ran. |
| [! Borderline]{.ck .ck-borderline} | A gate was flagged, meaning it ran but missed its criteria. An *i* means every flag has a documented cause, often a property of the method or of the comparison rather than of the implementation, and links to the notes below the table. |
| [✗ Fail]{.ck .ck-fail} | A gate errored or produced no valid result. |
| [⊘ Blocked]{.ck .ck-blocked} | The gates are excluded for a recorded reason that may be lifted: the solver is unstable on them, they are infeasible within the time or memory budget, an upstream bug stops them, or the wrapper does not implement them yet. The cell names the reason. |
| [— Not supported]{.ck .ck-na} | The method cannot express the experiment, e.g. a forward-only solver has no gradient. |
| [· Not run]{.ck .ck-notrun} | Not run in this campaign yet. |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Gate experiments per setup"}
{{< include _gates.qmd >}}

Some criteria are absolute, such as an error bound against an analytic solution
or a converged reference run, an observed order of convergence, or a minimum
agreement with finite differences. Others compare a solver with the other
solvers on the same experiment, for example an error more than three times the
median of its peers. A flag on a relative criterion says that a solver is an
outlier among its peers, which need not mean that it misses an accuracy the
task needs. The thresholds are provisional and will be refined with the solver
maintainers. They live next to each experiment in
`mosaic/benchmarks/problems/<problem>/config.py`.
:::

## Ranking {#ranking}

Mosaic ranks solvers metric by metric, on these deliberately simple setups,
with the given implementations and hardware. Within each device group above,
solvers that pass more checks come first, then faster ones, and the tables on
each setup's results page sort by the metric named in their caption. Mosaic
does not combine the metrics into a single score, because capabilities,
hardware targets and numerics vary too widely for one number to mean much, and
cost is only one of many things a user weighs. A ranking on one setup is not a
general verdict on a solver.

## Investigating patterns {#investigating-patterns}

Every solver runs the same experiments, so the results can be compared along
other lines than the setup. The [solver reference](solvers.qmd) lists each
solver's discretization, backend and AD strategy, which lets you group solvers
that share numerical characteristics. The experiment explorer below collects
the plots of every experiment, and comparing a setup's gradient checks with its
optimization outcomes can show how far gradient quality predicts optimization
performance. For your own analysis, the full result tree of every release is
attached to its [GitHub release](https://github.com/pasteurlabs/mosaic/releases)
as `mosaic-results-<version>.zip`. The [paper](paper.qmd) is a worked example of
this kind of investigation.
